description: Adults are 1.5 mm long, yellow abdomen and thorax, white wings; nymphs are oval, translucent or yellowish. Last instar is called 'red-eye nymph'.
hosts: Cole crops (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, kohlrabi, Chinese cabbage, brussels sprouts)
Other vegetable crops as incidental hosts
damage: Sap-sucking leads to stunted growth and delayed harvest
Excretion of honeydew promotes sooty mold, reducing photosynthesis
Bleaching of stems and leaf petioles in broccoli (white stem)
life_cycle: First instar (crawler) is mobile; subsequent nymphs are sessile
Adults fly readily when plants are disturbed
spread: By wind and migration from nearby crops
Mechanical spread via contaminated tools or workers
Rapid population increase when nearby hosts are declining
monitoring: Yellow sticky traps help detect initial migration
Turn over leaves to inspect nymphs

cultural: Delay planting or create host-free periods to reduce infestation
Plant crops upwind from other whitefly hosts
Maintain sanitation: remove weeds and crop residues promptly
Manage irrigation and nitrogen to avoid excessive plant growth favoring whiteflies
biological: Predators: bigeyed bugs, lacewing larvae, lady beetles
Entomopathogenic fungi: Beauveria bassiana, Isaria fumosorosea
organic: Beauveria bassiana and Isaria fumosorosea for nymph control
resistance_management: Rotate insecticides with different mode-of-action groups

notes: Thresholds are not well established; in organic or untreated fields, treat borders preferentially if infestation is higher at edges.
